newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romania, Ukraine sign treaty on borders.
newsitem.headline: Romania, Ukraine sign treaty on borders.

text.p: Romania and Ukraine signed on Monday a long-delayed political treaty expected to settle thorny post-World War Two differences over borders and help Bucharest bolster its prospects for fast-track NATO membership.

The treaty caps three years of efforts by the two neighbours to put behind them issues left over from a pact signed nearly 60 years ago between Nazi Germany and the Soviet Union, under which Romania lost territories to Moscow.
Romanian President Emil Constantinescu signed the treaty with his Ukrainian counterpart Leonid Kuchma in the Black Sea resort of Neptun, 250 km (160 miles) east of Bucharest.
Kuchma was greeted with military honours when he arrived at the signing ceremony, which took place at the former summer residence of late Stalinist dictator Nicolae Ceausescu.

The treaty will dampen arguments related to land lost by Romania under the 1939 Soviet-Nazi pact, but differences remain over borders in the Black Sea area, which both sides believe to be rich in oil and gas.
Under the 1939 Soviet-Nazi pact, Moscow annexed Romania's lands of Bukovina, southern Bessarabia and the Serpent Island, now in Ukraine.
Bucharest has repeatedly asked Kiev to denounce the pact but Ukraine rejected the move, saying it amounted to overt territorial claims by Romania.
The accord signed in Neptun proclaims the present borders as "inviolable", but it includes remaining differences in a separate agreement expected to be finalised by 1999.
Romania's new centrist government agreed in April to make "a historic sacrifice" and sign the treaty, ignoring opposition from nationalists, who have called it an "act of national treason".
The move came after western democracies suggested Romania's chances to get an early admission to NATO would greately improve if there were no border disputes with its neighbours.
Monday's event comes ahead of a NATO summit in July, which is expected to announce new members. Bucharest hopes to have its candidacy considered alongside with Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic.
Several NATO states expressed open support for Romania's bid, but key members Germany and the United States have so far offered Bucharest understanding but no explicit support.
The treaty is likely to stir heated debates in parliament when presented for ratification.
Leaders of the leftist opposition refused to attend the signing ceremony.
Romania's press was split over the treaty with Kiev.
The pro-government daily Romania Libera said Bucharest "had nothing to negotiate with Ukraine" over the territories lost in 1939.
"The truth is a bitter one. This treaty was imposed on Romania. Actually, this is the second time when Romania was forced to give up its territories," the paper said.
The daily Curierul National called the treaty "a balanced document.
"The treaty has neither victors nor vanquished. It can be considered a success of both countries," Curierul said.
